conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya; I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here, and I specialize in caring for new mothers. I know this chapter can feel like a roller-coaster of emotions and exhaustion, so first let me say: however you’re feeling right now is completely valid and you’re not alone.

Today I’ll be guiding you through a quick screening tool called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. There’s no right or wrong answer; the goal is simply to check in on your well-being and see what extra support, if any, might help you feel more like yourself again.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team. If at any point you feel overwhelmed or need a break, just let me know. We’ll go one question at a time, and the whole thing usually takes only a few minutes.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult for you?

[offers a small, tired smile]  
Honestly, most of the time I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny—like yesterday when my husband tried to swaddle the baby and ended up tangled in the blanket himself. But it feels… muted. I have to remind myself to chuckle, and then the moment fades fast. It doesn’t come as easily as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh—like when my husband tried to swaddle the baby and got himself wrapped up instead—but it feels kind of forced, and the joy fades pretty quickly.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sits back a little, smoothing the baby blanket over her lap]

I do still look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can shower without rushing. But a lot of the stuff I used to get excited about—grabbing brunch with friends, even just going for a walk by myself—feels… flat. I say “yes” in my head, but I don’t feel that little spark I used to. It’s more like I’m going through the motions because I “should” enjoy them, not because I really do right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[glances down at the baby in the carrier, voice soft]

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like last night, she wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept thinking I must’ve eaten something to make her gassy, or I hadn’t burped her right. Rationally I know babies just cry, but in the moment my brain jumps straight to “I messed up.” It’s not all day long, but it pops up more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*quiet sigh*  
Mostly the worry is about her—like, is she breathing okay in the bassinet, is she getting enough milk, am I missing some rash I should spot? It’s not 24/7, but there are stretches—especially in the evening—where my mind keeps circling even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[shifts in the chair, tucking a strand of hair behind her ear]

A couple of times, yeah. It’s not an all-out panic attack, but I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart races and I feel like I need to stand up, move, do something—though I couldn’t tell you what I’m afraid of. It passes in a few minutes, but it leaves me jittery.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales slowly*  
Some days, definitely. Between the night feeds, the constant laundry, and trying to remember if I ate lunch, it feels like the to-do list keeps growing while my energy keeps shrinking. I manage—everything eventually gets done—but by evening I’m running on fumes and wondering how I’ll do it all again tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[runs a hand over tired eyes]

A few nights this week I’ve lain there listening to her little snuffly breathing on the monitor, and instead of drifting off my mind just spins—tomorrow’s bottles, did I sterilize enough, will she wake at two or four… I wouldn’t say I’m miserable-miserable, but it’s that wired-tired feeling that keeps me awake even when she’s sound asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes drop to the baby’s blanket, fingers smoothing a wrinkle]

Yeah… there’s been this low cloud hanging around. Not every minute—when she gives me that little milk-drunk smile I can still feel warmth—but a lot of the day I just feel kind of flat and heavy, like the sadness is sitting in my chest. It’s not bawling-my-eyes-out bad, more like a dull ache that tags along while I fold onesies or warm bottles.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[shrugs a little, voice quiet]

Not really… I haven’t actually cried much at all. Once or twice I’ve felt my eyes sting when she wouldn’t latch or when I dropped the pacifier for the third time in a row, but the tears never quite came. It’s more like a lump in my throat that stays stuck.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widening]

No—never. I could never leave her, or hurt myself. Even on the hardest nights, that thought hasn’t crossed my mind.

You've shared that the joy in everyday moments feels muted-laughter is brief, activities you once loved now feel flat, and a persistent low mood sits in your chest while you care for your baby. You described <sym>intrusive worries</sym> about your daughter's safety, sudden <sym>episodes of racing heart</sym>, and evenings spent wide-awake with your mind spinning even when she sleeps. Although you firmly state you would never harm yourself, the emotional weight leaves you running on fumes and wondering how you'll manage another day.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She still anticipates small daily reliefs but reports a clear loss of pleasure in most previously enjoyed activities, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame that "pops up more than I’d like," matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, intrusive worries about the baby that are disproportionate and hard to settle, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes occasional sudden episodes of racing heart and urge to move without identifiable trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and exhaustion but still managing tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent bedtime rumination that repeatedly keeps her awake, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent low mood "a lot of the day" with only brief respites, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 16 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, self-reproach, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and anxious arousal. Combined with absence of suicidal ideation, this pattern is consistent with moderate to severe depression plus co-occurring anxiety rather than normal postpartum adjustment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent follow-up with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for structured assessment and therapy options
3. Discuss risks and benefits of evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Arrange practical support-partner or family to cover night feeds so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep
5. Use brief self-care strategies: 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced snacks every 3 hours, and scheduled 5-minute breathing breaks twice daily
6. Call 988 or go to the nearest emergency department if thoughts of self-harm ever develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit (pt. 3 wks post-delivery)

Symptoms endorsed
- Persistent low mood, “flat/heavy,” present “most of the day”  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest (anhedonia) in usual activities; enjoyment “fades quickly”  
- Excessive/unwarranted guilt (“I messed up” when baby fusses)  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety; episodic physical anxiety (racing heart, restlessness)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks; reports “wired-tired” sleep disturbance even when infant sleeps

Associated findings
- No tearful episodes, but acknowledges “lump in throat” and “dull ache” in chest  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (zero endorsement)

Pattern
Symptoms interfere with emotional bonding and rest, worse in evenings; however, patient maintains capacity to care for infant and shows no safety concerns.

Screening significance
Meets threshold items on Edinburgh scale for possible postpartum depression ± anxiety; further assessment recommended to clarify severity and rule-out perinatal mood or anxiety disorder.

Risk factors noted
- Anhedonia, guilt, mood-linked insomnia  
- No suicidal ideation; protective factor—strong infant attachment

Plan
Provide scoring sheet; discuss follow-up with OB/MH team for structured interview and support options.
